rationale: B wins because it finds one more real door into the story: “Databricks graded its own model, and that is the part enterprises should check” turns the weakest supplied fact into a reporter-shaped accountability angle. A is strong, but “For banks and hospitals, the AI question is custody, not capability” is mostly a cleaner rewrite of its closed-API regulated-customer angle, with a new hat and the same shoes. Both sets avoid the worst AI-launch sludge; B just does more useful damage with the facts on the table.
gaps_in_A: “For banks and hospitals” imports sectors not supplied in the update; plausible, but still an assumption dressed as a headline.
“cannot send sensitive data to a third-party API” overstates the evidence. The update says regulated enterprises and closed APIs, not an absolute compliance bar.
Angles 2 and 3 crowd each other: “closed-API vendors' regulated customers” and “custody, not capability” need the same customer proof and chase the same buyer story.
It refuses the bad benchmark-superiority angle but misses the sharper story hiding in plain sight: the benchmarks are company-run and therefore a verification problem.
gaps_in_B: “open weights mean third parties can begin reproducing them immediately” is an inference from open-sourcing/open license, not a fact supplied in the update.
“gives away for free” is too loose. An open license may still carry commercial restrictions, which the set itself admits reporters will check.
“banks, hospitals, and insurers” are plausible regulated buyers, but they are not in the update. Use them as examples, not assumed targets.
“No current news signal was supplied” overcorrects. The model release and revenue disclosure are the supplied news signal; what is missing is an external newsjack peg.
